entries.title: August 2026 Was the Hottest Month Ever Recorded: Copernicus Data
entries.summary: While the strengthening El Niño helped boost temperatures, climate change is the main culprit for making August so hot.
entries.content:
August was the planet’s hottest month ever recorded, capping a remarkably grim summer of heat records. With El Niño strengthening—and climate change continuing to heat things up—more records are likely in store well into next year.

Data from Copernicus, the European Union’s climate agency, shows that last month tied with July 2023 for Earth’s hottest month. (July is also usually the hottest month of the year.) This July also tied with July of 2024 for the second-hottest July on record, while June 2026 was the second-hottest June ever recorded. The news comes on the heels of a separate announcement on Wednesday from the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, which declared this was the hottest summer for the US, beating a previous record set during the Dust Bowl.

The sweltering summer is a grim sign of how burning fossil fuels is pushing temperatures up around the globe while unleashing more intense and longer heat waves.

“August 2026 was a remarkable month in the global climate record,” Samantha Burgess, the strategic lead for climate at the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts, said in a statement. “Combined with record global sea surface temperatures and the warmest summer on record for Western Europe, these observations show how climate change is driving extremes across both the atmosphere and the oceans. The impacts of these conditions are increasingly being felt by communities, economies and ecosystems across the world.”

The global average temperature for August was 1.65 degrees Celsius (3 degrees Fahrenheit) above the preindustrial average, according to Copernicus. While it was hot globally this summer, the impacts played out with dangerous and sometimes deadly results locally.

Researchers estimate that as many as 35,000 people died during heatwaves in Germany, France, and Spain alone this summer. Record-breaking fires also raged across parts of Europe, unleashing the first documented fire cloud in France and threatening a key NASA observatory in Spain. In North America, wildfires raging in Canada and northern parts of the US filled areas across the Northeast with smoke.

Climate change has boosted background temperatures, but the El Niño roiling the eastern Pacific Ocean has piled on more heat. El Niños usually coincide with a temporary uptick in global temperature between 0.1 to 0.2 degrees Celsius. This year’s El Niño is forecast to reach record strength and upend weather around the globe. But the full impact on the planet’s temperature won’t be felt until next year, meaning that next summer may be even hotter than the one we just lived through.

Climate scientists have warned that the world needs to prevent long-term average warming from breaching 1.5 degrees Celsius to avoid the worst impacts of climate change. While temperatures above the threshold for a single month don’t represent a permanent breach of this temperature, they’re a sign that the world is getting closer to this benchmark.

Earlier this month, the UN warned in a report that the world is likely to cross the 1.5 degrees Celsius threshold in a few years. To slow and eventually reverse the rise in global temperatures, the world needs to stop burning fossil fuels and lower carbon emissions.

“This summer’s scorching heat, raging wildfires and deadly floods are a warning of what lies ahead,” UN Secretary-General Antőnio Guterres said in a statement. “We must make the overshoot above 1.5 degrees as small and short as possible. That demands an overshoot of ambition.”

entries.title: Which iPhone 18 Model Should You Buy?
entries.summary: Apple’s new folding iPhone Duo is finally here, alongside refreshed Pro models. Our primer has all the details you need to choose the iPhone 18 that’s right for you.
entries.content:
With a fresh folding form factor, the new iPhone Duo is Apple’s most radical redesign in years. It lands alongside the more familiar-looking iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max. There’s no regular iPhone 18, or at least, not yet. Rumors suggest we may see a more affordable base model, perhaps flanked by an iPhone 18e and a second-generation iPhone Air, in spring 2027.

The two new Pro iPhones are available to preorder on September 12 and ship on September 18. You can preorder the iPhone Duo from October 16, ahead of a full release on October 23. But which iPhone 18 model is right for you? I’ll break down the differences and what these phones have in common, so you can choose with confidence. For options beyond the iPhone 18 lineup, read our Best iPhones guide.

Why You Might Not Need to Upgrade

Before you drop all those hard-earned dollars, remember that you probably don’t need the latest iPhone. If you have an older iPhone, Apple does a good job of updating the software (the iPhone 11 Pro is still supported), and for hardware issues, your iPhone might be repairable; maybe it needs a battery replacement or these troubleshooting tips. Don’t feel like you have to spring for Apple’s shiny new thing.

Sadly, Apple raised iPhone Pro prices this year, so both models are $100 more expensive than the iPhone 17 Pro series.

If you’re set on upgrading, consider raising funds by selling your old iPhone. Just be sure to back up your iPhone, and factory reset it before you sell or give it away. Once the new device arrives, we have tips on how to set up your new iPhone and what settings to change to get the most out of it.

Which iPhone 18 Is Right for You?

We’ll start by looking at what’s the same across the iPhone 18 models this year.

All three new iPhones have Apple’s A20 Pro chip inside, and, you guessed it, this is Apple’s most powerful chip ever. Now, iPhones are already the most capable phones for raw compute power, but the A20 Pro promises a significant jump in performance (around 20 percent faster and 30 percent more efficient than the last generation). It also packs a new neural engine to power on-device AI and a new thermal design with a larger vapor chamber to keep things cool. For the iPhone Duo, the A20 Pro has a display engine to ensure smooth transitions between two screens. While Apple doesn’t list the RAM, every model is rumored to have 12 GB.

While they come in different sizes and the Duo has two, every iPhone features an OLED screen that Apple calls a Super Retina XDR display. They also have ProMotion technology, otherwise known as a 120-Hz refresh rate. These adaptive refresh rates can drop as low as 1 Hz when there's little activity on the screen, enabling features like the always-on display without draining the battery too much.

The displays are protected by the scratch-resistant and antireflective Ceramic Shield 2, the same as last year’s iPhone 17 range. And they can go from 1 nit up to 3,000 nits of brightness. Only the iPhone Duo has a custom nano-texture finish on the interior screen, giving it a matte look that’s designed to reduce glare and crease visibility.

All the phones have an IP68 rating for water and dust resistance, meaning they can survive a short dunk in fresh water. They all come in four storage options (256 GB, 512 GB, 1 TB, or 2 TB), support Qi2 magnetic wireless charging (MagSafe), USB-C 3.2, Dual SIM, Wi-Fi 7, Bluetooth 6, Thread, and Ultra-Wideband (UWB). It also has Siri AI, Apple Intelligence, Emergency SOS via Satellite, and Crash Detection.

To help you better understand which model to buy, here's precisely where they diverge.

Apple has taken its time with its first foldable, enabling it to learn from the best folding phones already on the market. Eschewing the more prevalent book- and flip-style foldables, Apple has gone with a passport-sized form factor for the iPhone Duo, similar to Samsung's recent Galaxy Z Fold8 (our current favorite). The Duo has a 5.4-inch screen on the outside, but unfolds to reveal a 7.6-inch display inside that feels like an iPad Mini.

The iPhone Duo has a tough titanium frame, a precision hinge with magnets for that satisfying snap-shut, and an IP68 rating for solid dust and water resistance. But at 254 grams and 11.3 mm thick when folded, and 5.2 mm unfolded, the Duo is not the slimmest or lightest foldable around (the Fold8 is 201 grams, 9.7 mm thick folded, and 4.5 mm unfolded).

Foldables don’t have as much space for cameras, so the Duo drops Face ID (Touch ID is in the side power button instead) and makes do without a telephoto lens (you get a 48-megapixel primary camera and a 48-megapixel ultrawide). But it has room for the biggest-ever iPhone battery, promising 24 hours of mixed use.

Where Apple will likely add a lot of value to the foldable phone category is with its software design. Controls have been pushed to the side and stacked vertically to free up more screen real estate. Apps offer plenty of split-screen support, and transitions between displays look slick. Apple has also included features that take advantage of the fact that you can prop the Duo open on a table or nightstand, so there’s StandBy support to use the outer screen as an alarm clock, while the inside display gently pulses with light to wake you.

Who it’s for: You want something different. You’re curious about folding phones or already convinced they’re great and can’t wait to experience Apple’s take.

The iPhone 18 Pro is similar to last year’s 17 Pro, with a 6.3-inch display, though the Dynamic Island has been slightly slimmed and can now show three Live Activities notifications at once. It keeps the same aluminum unibody, with Ceramic Shield on the back glass, Ceramic Shield 2 on the front, and an IP68 rating. Black is back, and there’s also a new Burgundy color, alongside Glacier and Silver. Those colors look more uniform than the 17 Pro’s two-tone finish.

Two standout upgrades stand out: The new A20 Pro chipset is faster and more power-efficient, and the main camera now has a variable aperture. The A20 Pro also enables better on-device AI and is aided by a redesigned vapor chamber to keep it cool while it works. Apple reckons you can expect 34 hours of video playback; that’s three hours more than the 17 Pro.

The camera introduces a physical lens aperture. Like the pupil of your eye, the aperture is the lens opening that lets light in. A bigger aperture can let in more light for better photos when it’s darker, and a smaller aperture can help you avoid overly bright photos when the sun is shining. But the aperture also impacts depth of field, so a bigger aperture can help you achieve that bokeh blurred background effect for a portrait photo, while a smaller aperture can help retain detail across a wider landscape shot. The camera app has new features and controls to help you take advantage of it.

Who it’s for: You don't want a big phone, but you want full-strength Apple silicon, a top camera, and all the latest features.

If foldables aren’t for you, the iPhone 18 Pro Max offers the biggest screen you can get at 6.9 inches, and it is a battery-life beast. Apple says you can get up to 43 hours of video playback out of a full charge; that’s a six-hour increase on last year’s already impressive 17 Pro Max. It has the same design and colors as the regular Pro, just bigger.

You also get the new chip and variable aperture camera. Both Pro models now boast a versatile triple 48-megapixel camera system with pro controls for lens aperture, shutter speed, and white balance. The class-leading video capture goes up to 4K at 120 fps. The iPhone 18 Pro phones are the right pick for photographers and videographers.

Who it’s for: You want the best Apple has to offer, including a big screen and long battery life, in a familiar form factor.

How to Get the iPhone 18 Unlocked

It makes sense to buy your iPhone unlocked, since it's much easier to switch carriers or use an international eSIM when you travel. The iPhones sold through Apple's storefront are unlocked, so Apple.com is the best place to buy them. During a preorder period, you can only purchase a newly announced iPhone from Apple.

Don't forget to take advantage of Apple's promotions: You get three free months of Apple One, which includes Apple Music, Apple TV+, Apple Arcade, News+, Apple Fitness+, and extra iCloud storage. Just watch out, because it will auto-bill you after the trial. Set a reminder to cancel if you don't want to continue subscribing to these services.

  • The iPhone Duo starts at $1,999 for 256 GB
  • The iPhone 18 Pro starts at $1,199 for 256 GB
  • The iPhone 18 Pro Max starts at $1,299 for 256 GB

Apple has some financing options. If you have an Apple Card, you can pay for your iPhone over 24 months at 0-percent APR, and most carriers offer financing deals, too. Apple also offers Apple Upgrade, enabling you to lease your new iPhone from $35 a month for 24 months for the entry-model iPhone 18 Pro (12 months starts at $50 a month). We don’t think it’s a good deal, but if you’re tempted, remember you must return it in good condition (AppleCare+ with Theft and Loss costs an extra $15 a month).

entries.title: Best Robot Lawn Mowers (2026): 12+ Models Tested Over 3 Years
entries.summary: Smart mowers are an expensive alternative to old-fashioned yard work, but they’re finally good enough to consider if you’d rather sip an iced tea and watch a robot tame your lawn.
entries.content:
Featured in this article

Lawn care is a monotonous, thankless task. Who wants to mow the lawn when you could be lollygagging in a hammock with a cold drink, watching a robot do it for you? That’s right: no one. Robot lawn mowers were once the preserve of the wealthy, and yes, they can still be on the pricey side. But they’re getting cheaper and better all the time.

I’ve tested a handful of the best robot lawn mowers over the past three years, and after comparing a fresh crop this mowing season, I'm delighted to tell you that robot mowers are actually good now. I've got some recommendations, honorable mentions, and a list of robot mowers you should avoid. Read on for everything you need to know about lawn-tending bots.

Updated September 2026: I added mowers from Roborock, Segway, Eufy, and Sunseeker, added information about night mowing to the FAQ, and updated prices.

Other Robot Mowers I Tested and Liked

Roborock Rockmow X120H Lidar for $3,200: Better known for its robot vacuums, Roborock also makes robot mowers, and the X120H Lidar is its flagship model (discounted to a far more reasonable $2,000 at the time of writing). I actually tested the UK model, the identical Z120 Lidar (£2,299). This mower employs Lidar and AI vision, so it can cut without satellite connections, with no RTK antenna required. It also supports 4G and comes with a 3-year data plan. It is Four Wheel Drive (4WD) and has ingenious front wheels that pivot and turn independently to navigate tight areas smoothly, with minimal churning of your lawn. There’s a single disc underneath with six cutting blades and a reasonably wide, 9.5-inch (24 cm) cutting width. It supports a 0.8 to 2.7-inch (20 to 70 mm) cutting height, can cover up to around 21,500 square feet, and, most impressively, can handle an 80 percent (up to 39-degree) slope. A full charge gives you 110 minutes of mowing time, and it takes around 50 minutes to charge.

After some minor setup hassles (battery error), the Rockmow Z120 has impressed me. It looks to be the most capable mower I have tested yet for navigating uneven terrain. Apparently, it can automatically create maps, but it defaulted to the manual mode for me, prompting me to remote control it around the borders of my lawn. Edge mowing is the big disappointment, with the mower regularly leaving a strip on one edge of my lawn. I’m not keen on the optional PreciEdge Module (£150) that promises to reduce edges to 3 cm. I haven’t tested it, but feel it should be included in a mower this expensive. Why is it optional? Who doesn’t want their edges properly cut? It avoided most obstacles just fine, but was occasionally oversensitive, avoiding plants swaying over the border edge. The Rain Protection mode is a little too sensitive, preventing the mower from starting several hours after rain, so I had to override it. It also lacks a Spot Mode, though it is so heavy I would not want to carry it between lawn areas. I think this design, with the rotating wheels, has real potential if Roborock can improve the AI/software. Unfortunately, it's not currently available in the US right now, but hopefully be back in stock soon since it was released just this past summer.

Eufy Robot Lawn Mower E15 for $1,300: This is another wire-free mower that uses a camera system to automatically map lawns and avoid obstacles. It’s very similar to my top pick and also has a super handy Spot Mode that lets you drop and mow on unmapped areas. But even after a big price drop from its original RRP, it’s still more expensive than the TerraMow, and it’s not as good at cutting edges. It can cover up to 0.2 acres (8,700 square feet), cut from 1 to 3 inches, and handle up to 18-degree slopes. It is also fairly quiet and has GPS tracking, but you must have Wi-Fi coverage in your backyard, or you'll need a 4G data subscription. I found the setup lengthy due to a firmware download, but the mapping and the first cut were decent. Object avoidance is very good. The E15 can only run during the day and doesn't cope very well with inclines. I also found it frequently failed to cut the edges of the lawn and doesn't perform well if the grass is damp. The more affordable Eufy C15 (£999) is very similar, but designed for smaller lawns (up to 5,300 square feet) and only available in the UK and Europe right now.

It kept my back lawn neat without issues, but my front lawn has a dip and ill-defined border that it struggled with. That said, every time it looked as though it might get stuck, it managed to maneuver out of trouble. There’s a dial to adjust mowing height for the C15, whereas you can do it in the app with the E15. Both come with a covered charging base, which often costs extra with rivals. If you’re interested, watch out for a sale event (I’ve seen the E15 drop below $1,000, which makes it far more tempting).

Segway Navimow X430 for $2,249: My backyard is both a Wi-Fi and 5G dead zone. Before manually mowing the yard I save all my podcasts and music to offline mode, and I let my fiancee know she’ll need to deploy a carrier pigeon if she needs to get my attention. So, it was a relief to see just how quickly the navigation system of the Navimow X430 recognized the unit across the treacherous triple lot that surrounds my house. It connected within seconds of beginning the initial setup and 20 minutes later, the robot mower was on its way using the handy auto-mapping function. As it turns out, I didn't need the three beers I'd brought with me when I embarked upon this process, assuming it would be on par with the weeks-long headache it took to get the Mammotion Luba 2 connected and operational last summer.

It did an above-average job on its first pass despite the endless flurry of compost piles, stray bushes, fencing and detritus from half-finished gardening projects that litter my half-acre lawn, though I opted for manual mapping to take advantage of its aptitude at hugging the wobbly brick borders of some raised beds with relative ease. The sites claims that it can handle “tall, thick and dense grass," which I had the perfect scenario to test. After a two weeks of dealing with an endless cycle of torrential downpours and blistering heat, I was left with few open windows for a good mow before my patchy, crabby grass got too unwieldy for the Navimow’s 4-inch height maximum. I watched with disappointment as it casually drove over some stray blades that went to seed without making any impact whatsoever. Despite that, the Navimow X430 has impressed me with its ease-of-use. We'll update our impressions here with additional testing, but so far so good.—Pete Cottell

Sunseeker X7 Gen 2 Wireless Robot Lawn Mower for $2,700: If you have a large, challenging lawn, this could be a mower worth considering. It combines built-in NET-RTK, GPS, and AI vision, has floating dual disc blades for uneven terrain, and can work at night thanks to an Indirect Time of Flight camera. It is also all-wheel drive (AWD) and can handle 70 percent slopes up to 35 degrees. It can cover more than 32,000 square feet. I love the wide 14-inch cutting width, the relatively quiet operation (it never went over 60 decibels but was usually even quieter), even though I’d advise against mowing at night because of the risk to wildlife. Sadly, the automatic mapping was mediocre, and there’s no Spot Mode for a drop-and-mow. This Gen 2 mower brings a raft of improvements over the original, including night vision, faster processing, enhanced durability and traction, a built-in screen, and onboard RTK without a separate antenna. But only the original Sunseeker X7 ($2,700) is available to buy on Amazon. You currently have to go through a dealer to get the Gen 2.

Husqvarna Aspire R6V for £999: While the reliable Husqvarna 410XE Nera was my top pick for a long time, you can get more affordable mowers now, without the hassle of RTK antennas. The Husqvarna Aspire R6V is just such a mower. It uses a combination of GPS and AI vision with a camera on the front. It was easy to set up and map the lawn in the app, but you will need a good Wi-Fi signal across your yard for it to work effectively. I was a little disappointed in the sensitive obstacle avoidance, as it left large uncut strips around the edges of my lawn. I was able to reduce the verge a little with some tinkering, but it was still larger than the recommendations above. Note: This model is currently not available in the US.

Anthbot Genie 3000 for $900: This often-discounted mower was my budget pick for a while, but mowers have moved on, so you can get better performance without the satellite antenna now. It offers auto-mapping, but the remote-control option works better. The mower cut my lawn effectively, but even after repeated map updates, it left an uncut verge. The obstacle avoidance works well, and it cuts in neat lines. It had no issues returning to charge or following a schedule. The voice that says it has connected or started mowing began to annoy me, but thankfully, it can be turned off. There were some glitches with rain alerts that prevented it from mowing, even long after the rain had stopped. I also experienced some flaky connection issues with the GPS, and it occasionally got stuck. While there is support for multiple areas, the mower often struggled picking up a signal in my front yard. Ultimately, this is still a decent mower when discounted, provided you have a modest-sized, straightforward lawn.

Mova Lidax 2000 for $1,199: With a sleek design and a mixture of 360-degree lidar for 3D mapping and a camera with AI vision, this mower proved very effective. Setup was straightforward, and there’s no need for wires or an antenna, though I did have to adjust the map manually. You can set multiple areas, and its navigation is generally very good. It mowed in neat lines, successfully avoided thin posts for the badminton net and other obstacles, and completed an excellent edge pass at the end. With some of the closest edge mowing I’ve seen, I was all set to recommend this mower, but then it got stuck. A couple of times, it seemed to be stuck, then managed to free itself, but an uneven problem spot proved to be its nemesis, and it chewed up a patch of grass trying to get free. Eventually, I had to make that spot a no-go zone. This mower is still worth considering, particularly if you see it on sale; just be prepared to tweak the map. The 2000 covers up to half an acre. If you have a quarter of an acre or less, the Mova Lidax 1000 ($1,299) is much cheaper but has the same features.

Avoid These Mowers

Stiga A6V: I like that this mower only needs the charging station and has no need for an antenna. The buggy setup was my first red flag, as a firmware update failed and had to be repeated. Once up and running, I found the mower always left a big verge, even after adjustment. The AI vision camera is very slow to react to obstacles and not very good at navigating around them. It hit the ball several times in my test, and I had to hit the stop button as it got too close to my cat. It lacks useful features like automapping and spot-mow, and there are better options for the money above. The yellow finish is a bit garish for my tastes too.

EcoFlow Blade: While it was easy to set up and cut my lawn nicely without the need for any boundary wire, the EcoFlow Blade sometimes struggled with GPS navigation and ended up stuck in a flower bed. It also left an untouched strip around the edge of my lawn. The object avoidance was solid, and it can be automated in the app, though it occasionally failed to start a scheduled cut for me. EcoFlow seems to have discontinued this model, though it is still on sale in Europe. Probably best to avoid.

Yardcare E400: Curious about the budget end of the robot mower market, I agreed to try the Yardcare E400, but this mower was an unmitigated disaster from start to finish. It’s a boundary wire model, so you must run wire around the area you want mowed. Yardcare suggests it can cover up to 4,300 square feet and cut grass between 0.8 and 2.4 inches. The problem is that it gets stuck frequently and struggles to even get on and off its charging station reliably. After trying multiple fixes to no avail and going through customer support, I had to conclude that this model has a serious design flaw.

How Do Robot Lawn Mowers Work?

Perhaps counterintuitively, the setup instructions for your robot lawn mower will likely tell you to start by cutting the grass. Robot mowers mostly can’t deal with long grass. Unlike traditional mowers, these robots don’t collect grass cuttings; they mulch instead, and they are designed to cut frequently, keeping your lawn short and simply leaving the cuttings on the ground, which can also improve lawn health. Most robot mowers are designed to run two or three times a week during the growing season (from late spring to early fall).

They have rechargeable batteries onboard and can last from half an hour to several hours on a full charge. They return to the charging base and recharge automatically when their power runs low. Most mowers have simple controls, a small display, and an emergency stop button. You can generally start and stop mowing, set schedules, and create or edit mapped areas using the onboard controls or the companion mobile app, very much like a robot vacuum.

What Features Should I Look For in a Robot Mower?

There are many factors to consider in choosing a robot mower, and the best choice for you often depends on your yard.

Robot lawn mowers are generally rated to cover a specific square footage, with wider coverage requiring models with larger batteries. Alongside yard size, you should consider the shape and topography of your lawn, as most robot mowers will struggle with steep inclines. While you can often map out separate areas so your robot mower can mow front and back lawns, for example, it will generally need you to lift and carry it between those areas. If you have an uneven garden or steep slopes, look for a four-wheel-drive (4WD) or all-wheel-drive (AWD) mower and check the manufacturer's rating for inclines.

There are a few types of navigation that robot mowers employ. We’ve tested five different approaches, though some mowers combine multiple technologies for better performance.

  • Satellite: Often employing something called Real-Time Kinematic (RTK) Global Positioning System (GPS), these mowers need a satellite signal to navigate and will have a receiver that must be placed in the open with a clear line of sight to the sky. Satellite navigation mowers are not suitable for areas with tall trees or buildings.
  • Light Detection and Ranging (lidar): This technology sends out rapid laser pulses to 3D map the terrain (it is also used by self-driving cars). It enables mowers to cut grass under thick tree canopies or near tall buildings where GPS signals usually fail.
  • Cameras: Cameras and onboard AI are used for obstacle detection and avoidance. AI vision can automatically map areas and cut the grass while avoiding obstacles it encounters, much like how most robot vacuums navigate a home to clean the floors.
  • Wire boundary: These mowers require you to install a perimeter wire as a boundary around your lawn that marks out the border the mower should not cross. It's a messy job that can be tricky.
  • Remote control: You mow your lawn from the comfort of your home using a remote controller or an app on your phone. Some only work via remote control, while others can also cut automatically.

Robot mowers generally come with large charging docks, and you’ll need to earmark a suitable spot for yours. They usually have extensive weatherproof cabling, but you will have to find a route to an outdoor socket.

To connect to your mower and schedule a mow, update the firmware, or remote control it where supported, you need a decent Wi-Fi signal or a Bluetooth connection. It’s best to set up your mower’s charging station within range of your Wi-Fi network. Some mowers also need a strong Wi-Fi signal to operate effectively, so you might consider adding an outdoor mesh router. If you want to connect your phone via Bluetooth, you will have to get quite close.

How Noisy Are Robot Mowers?

Most robot mowers are far quieter than their traditional counterparts. You can expect them to operate at around 55 decibels, though they may go as high as 75 decibels. We only tested battery-powered mowers, but expect gas mowers to be louder. While the operation is often quiet, I did find that several mowers made annoying beeping sounds when backing up or had a loud recorded voice during setup or upon receiving a command.

Do Robot Mowers Work in Any Weather?

Robot mowers and their charging stations usually have IP ratings and can cope with rain, but you should pack up and bring your mower indoors during the winter months. Many robot mowers have some kind of rain sensor and will pause mowing when it gets too wet. Some mowers may need to be paused manually. The wheels can churn up your lawn and get caked in mud if mowers continue to labor in the rain, especially with larger and heavier models.

How Well Do Robot Mowers Cut?

Mowers of different sizes will have varying cutting widths, denoting the width of the strip they can cut on each pass. Most also have floating cutting decks that enable you to choose the length of grass you want (typically 1 to 3 inches). Many robot mowers seem to struggle with cutting around the edges of a lawn, especially if there’s a wall or fence that prevents them from getting close enough.

It’s common to find an uncut verge around the edge of your lawn, so you might need to occasionally get the string trimmer out. Every robot mower I’ve tested has also struggled to cut the area around the charging station, so I recommend placing the unit on a deck or pavement if possible.

Can I Install a Robot Mower Myself?

​Yes, most robot mowers can be installed by anyone, but you might want to set aside an afternoon to work out any snags. Finding the best spot for the receiver for a satellite mower can be tricky. The mapping process can also take a while; usually, the mower will prompt you to remote-control it around the border you want to set. After the first mow, you should review its performance and make tweaks to ensure it’s covering the entire area you want to cut.

Can Robot Mowers Mow at Night?

Some models are capable of mowing at night in the dark using headlights, Lidar, and Time of Flight sensors, alongside their usual navigation capabilities. This can be convenient and also removes the risk for pets or children playing on the lawn during the day. However, there is a risk of injuring nocturnal wildlife, like hedgehogs in the UK and Europe. Mowers are also more likely to make mistakes and get stuck in the dark. It may be better to schedule mowing for dawn or dusk.

How I Test Robot Lawn Mowers

I test each robot lawn mower for at least a month, on at least two different lawn areas, assessing the ease of setup, the mapping process, automatic scheduling (where available), navigation, obstacle avoidance, and the quality of the final cut, looking for length, uniformity, and any missed patches. Where applicable, I try extra features, tweak settings in the app, and check how the mower handles different weather conditions. I also keep an eye on battery performance and charging time to ensure it aligns with the manufacturer's claims.

entries.title: Charlie Kirk Was Shot a Year Ago. The Conspiracy Theories Are More Rampant Than Ever
entries.summary: Experts say conspiracy theorizing about the identity and motive of Charlie Kirk’s killer will likely continue for a long time to come.
entries.content:
In the days after the assassination of conservative activist and Turning Point cofounder Charlie Kirk, the online reaction was a mess. Graphic videos of the shooting were everywhere within minutes of his death, far-right figures called for violence and vengeance, and right-wing lawmakers and influencers called for the cancellation—and worse—of anyone celebrating. Then, the conspiracy theories began.

It’s been one year since Kirk’s death, and conspiracy theories about the shooting have persisted, supercharged by social media algorithms and right-wing influencers like Candace Owens, who has used her huge following to push baseless allegations about the incident.

Experts believe these conspiracy theories will continue for a long time to come. “There’s no reason to believe conspiracy theories about Kirk’s murder will lose steam anytime soon,” Jared Holt, senior researcher at Open Measures, tells WIRED. “If anything, I expect them to escalate further as the criminal trial against Tyler Robinson, the man accused of killing Kirk, plays out over the next year or so. The trial is bound to draw major media attention and offer conspiracy theorists a source of new material to work from.”

In the immediate aftermath of Kirk’s death, some conspiracy theorists claimed the assassination was a false flag operation designed to deflect attention away from President Donald Trump’s connections to Jeffrey Epstein. Others claimed the entire thing was staged. There was the AI-powered gun theory, the claim that the shooter was a Kirk supporter, and even claims that Kirk was still alive.

But ultimately, the baseless claim that persisted is that someone close to Kirk, or operating on behalf of Israel, was responsible for his death, that Robinson was simply a patsy, and what really killed Kirk was an exploding microphone. This is the narrative that has been central to Owens’ monthslong conspiracy theory campaign. Her Kirk content has racked up hundreds of millions of views.

Owens’ success is fueled in large part by the way that social media platforms today encourage their users to post content. “X and YouTube are rife with speculation about Kirk’s death, where it is both still possible to recruit new audiences and monetize them,” Joan Donovan, assistant professor of journalism and emerging media studies at Boston University, tells WIRED.

The result is that Kirk’s death has become yet another rabbit hole, or a way for viewers to distract themselves from reality. “Candace and other conspiratorial influencers make things seem much more mysterious and exciting,” Renée DiResta, an associate research professor at Georgetown University who tracks disinformation, tells WIRED. “For many, her explanations are preferable to the reality of an act of violence by a solo individual.”

There have already been real-world repercussions: Researchers at the Network Contagion Research Institute recently found that “Candace Owens caused a measurable, statistically significant surge in death threats and calls for violence against [Charlie Kirk’s wife] Erika Kirk.” In May, a man was arrested for allegedly threatening to kill Erica Kirk ahead of her appearance at a Turning Point USA event in San Antonio, though the man has yet to be charged. Owens did not respond to a request for comment.

Erica Kirk and Turning Point have repeatedly called for Owens and others to stop spreading baseless rumors about the assassination. While those calls have not been heeded, Turning Point believes the impact the conspiracy theories are having is fading.

“The conspiracy theories have much less reach and potency now than they did six months ago, and I think I’ll say the same six months from now,” Andrew Kolvet, a Turning Point spokesperson, tells WIRED. “They won’t stop because many of these personalities were completely unknown and broke before Charlie was killed, and this is their moneymaker, but their influence and credibility have collapsed and will continue to do so.”

But some experts disagree, arguing that conspiratorial thinking has been an aspect of American life for decades.

“Historically, this is quite normal,” Joseph Uscinski, professor of political science at the University of Miami and author of American Conspiracy Theories, tells WIRED. “Majorities of Americans have believed for decades that JFK was killed by a conspiracy rather than by a lone gunman. In fact, almost 80 percent of Americans believed in the 1970s there was a conspiracy behind the assassination.”

entries.title: Best Bluetooth Speaker (2026): JBL, Sonos, Marshall, and More
entries.summary: I tested portable speakers of all shapes and sizes, from pocket to party-sized.
entries.content:
If you want to bring your music everywhere, the humble Bluetooth speaker is your best bet. You’ll lose some audio quality compared to bookshelf speakers, but these days, Bluetooth speakers sound pretty great, and let you blast the tunes wherever you go—the backyard, the beach, and beyond.

Since they first appeared on the audio scene back in 2010, the team at WIRED has reviewed hundreds of Bluetooth speakers at every price range. My top pick for most use cases remains the portable, durable, and affordable JBL Flip 7 ($150), but I’ve got specialized recommendations for nearly every use case and budget. From outdoor parties, beach days and poolside fun, to at-home listening in every room, these are the best speakers for everything you do.

Don’t forget to check out WIRED’s other audio guides, including the Best Soundbars, Best Wireless Earbuds, and Best Computer Speakers.

Updated September 2026: I’ve added the LG xboom Stage 501 and JBL Go 5 to my recommendations, refreshed the Honorable Mentions list, and updated pricing and copy with the most up to date information.

How I Test Bluetooth Speakers

WIRED’s audio experts have spent countless hours listening to, carrying, charging, dropping, and dunking Bluetooth speakers. I’ve been testing audio equipment for more than 20 years and remember the excitement surrounding the launch of the industry-changing Jawbone Jambox way back in 2010. It helped take wireless speakers mainstream and kick-started an entire industry. Since then, I’ve lost count of the number of Bluetooth speakers I’ve tested, but looking around my office today, I count at least 20 cluttering up the place.

Every speaker gets extensive listening with a wide mix of music, podcasts, and recordings of varying quality, including basic Spotify streams and high-resolution lossless audio from Qobuz and Tidal. This guide focuses on portable, battery-powered speakers, so there are inevitable compromises in sound compared to hi-fi speakers, but the difference between the best and worst is still remarkable.

Where possible, I compare similarly priced and sized speakers directly. A $50 speaker does not need to compete with a $500 one, but it does need to outperform the alternatives you might realistically buy instead.

I also test portability, controls, apps, Bluetooth reliability, useful extras, and battery life against manufacturers’ claims. The latter takes increasingly ridiculous amounts of time these days, especially with many speakers breaching the 50 hour mark.

And if a brand says its speaker is built for the beach, backyard, or pool, I test that too. Admittedly, WIRED doesn’t get as many pool days as it would like, but there’s always the bath.

What Should I Look for in a Bluetooth Speaker?

That entirely depends on what you plan to use it for. The best advice we have is to start with how and where you’d like to listen to music and work backwards to a specific model from there. Speakers include tiny keychains, larger boomboxes, and everything in between. We select speakers based largely on how they perform in their specialty, whether that’s audio quality, durability, or some other particular niche.

As far as durability, we look for speakers with solid IP ratings for dust and water resistance and tend to prefer long battery life; batteries with larger capacities tend to still work well even after a few years of degradation.

Best Bluetooth Speaker Overall

Specs

Battery Life Up to 14 hours (16 in boost mode)
Dust/Water Resistance IP68
Connectivity Bluetooth, USB-C charging
Special Features Auracast multispeaker, stereo pairing
Dimensions 7.2 x 2.7 x 2.8 inches
Weight 1.23 pounds

Small enough to go almost anywhere but big enough to let you properly enjoy your music, the JBL Flip 7 hits a sweet spot that makes it an easy recommendation. It sounds remarkably good for something this compact (and affordable), with plenty of bass and punch, clear vocals, and refined detail. Build quality is excellent too, with IP68 water and dust protection and some drop-proofing (within reason)..

JBL keeps improving the Flip with every iteration. It now has 14 hours of battery life (or 16 with the bass-reducing Playtime Boost mode), and Auracast lets you link newer compatible JBL speakers together for a surround sound experience. The app also has a useful seven-band EQ if you like to tinker with your tones.

As a nice bonus for those who care about bit rates, the Flip 7 can play 24-bit/96kHz lossless audio if you plug it into a source via the USB-C, which is a surprising extra feature at this price point. JBL continues to be the brand to beat in the land of Bluetooth speakers.

Best Smart Bluetooth Speaker

Specs

Battery Life Up to 24 hours
Dust/Water Resistance IP67
Connectivity Bluetooth, Wi-Fi, USB-C charging
Special Features Sonos multiroom, Trueplay Audio adjustment, built-in voice commands
Dimensions 7.57 x 4.43 x 3.02 inches
Weight 2.87 pounds

If your house is already full of Sonos speakers, the Sonos Play is an easy addition to justify, with ample smarts and connectivity built-in. It sounds significantly better than the smaller Sonos Roam 2, with an audio performance closer to the brand’s excellent Sonos Era 100, despite being battery powered.

Wi-Fi connectivity means access to the full Sonos ecosystem and app, including more than 100 streaming services, voice control, automatic Trueplay tuning, and multiroom playback. Leave it on the supplied charging base and it’s a great Sonos speaker. Pick it up and switch to Bluetooth, and you have a portable speaker with a huge 24 hours of battery life and IP67 protection.

At 2.9 pounds, it’s just about portable enough for travel, although I was very aware I was carrying it in my backpack. You can also charge your phone from it or add an analog source using Sonos’ optional line-in adapter. If you’re already invested in Sonos’ ecosystem, and don’t mind a regularly-changing Sonos app, it’s hard to think of a more smart speaker.

Best Budget Bluetooth Speaker

Specs

Battery Life Up to 8 hours (10 in Boost Mode)
Dust/Water Resistance IP68
Connectivity Bluetooth 6.0, USB-C lossless audio
Special Features Auracast, AirTouch stereo pairing, 7-band app EQ, ambient edge lighting, Playtime Boost
Dimensions 3.98 x 3.05 x 1.7 inches
Weight 0.51 pounds

Great looks, cute size, and instantly stolen by my tweenage daughter, the Go 5 is my ideal tiny speaker. It weighs next to nothing and fits in the palm of my hand, but the 4.8 watt output sounds considerably less weedy than it has any right to.

The already excellent JBL Go 4 is a little cheaper, but the Go 5 brings fuller, deeper bass, clear mids, and enough punch to make music sound good. Its tough little enclosure is drop-proof and IP68 dust and waterproof. Connectivity is also impressive with Bluetooth 6.0, Auracast, 7-band app EQ, and clever pairing (where you bump two Go 5s together to create a stereo pair).

It’s speakers like this that remind me just how we’ve come since the days of sticking my phone in a mug to amplify the tiny built-in speaker. If only I knew where my daughter had put it.

Best Bluetooth Speaker for Battery Life

Specs

Battery Life 50+ hours
Dust/Water Resistance IP54
Connectivity Bluetooth 5.3, Auracast, AAC, 3.5mm AUX input and USB-C charging
Special Features True Stereophonic 360-degree sound, Dynamic Loudness, Bluetooth Multipoint, M-button presets, Marshall app
Dimensions 10.74 x 5.9 x 6.65 inches
Weight 6.17 pounds

I’m happy to admit when I’m wrong, and for a few years, I dismissed Marshall’s mini guitar amp aesthetic as a good looking gimmick. But having spent time with the Kilburn III, I hold my hands up. It’s not "serious" hi-fi, but the design and attention to detail—the tactile, spring-loaded, knurled metal power lever, and illuminated control knobs are a joy—stand apart. It just looks fantastic, and with 50 watts of power and 50 hours of playtime, it plays loud and long. I love being able to charge devices from the speaker’s USB-C port too.

Marshall does not include the charger needed for the fastest recharge, which is a bit annoying, although most laptop users will have one already. There’s no stereo pairing option either, but I find it hard to imagine needing two of these in the size of room it’s designed for.

In his Marshall Kilburn III review, reviewer Simon Cohen was ebullient about the speaker’s performance, and I agree. It’s loud enough for small- to medium-sized rooms, and cut through when used outdoors, with weighty bass, decent balance, and no obvious distortion when pushed. The 360-degree presentation spreads music evenly too, so it feels less directional than many rivals.

Best Bluetooth Speaker for Sound Quality

Specs

Battery Life Up to 24 hours
Dust/Water Resistance IP67
Connectivity Bluetooth 5.4, aptX Adaptive, AAC, SBC, Auracast, USB-C audio and charging
Special Features True Wireless Stereo pairing, Google Fast Pair, Microsoft Swift Pair, speakerphone with noise and echo cancellation
Dimensions 8.5 x 3.2 x 2.3 inches
Weight 1.6 pounds

Paying $250 for a portable Bluetooth speaker is hard to justify if all you need is something loud enough for a picnic blanket, but the Kef Muo feels more like a compact hi-fi component. The seamless aluminum body is beautifully tactile and flawless, although it looks almost identical to the model they first launched in 2015. Maybe I’m just feeling old because I remember that launch like it was yesterday.

While the Muo is getting on a bit aesthetically, its connectivity is bang up to date. The drivers have been rebuilt around a new racetrack-shaped 2.5 x 5-inch mid/bass driver, paired with a 0.74-inch (19mm) tweeter and 40W of Class D amplification. A neat pleated edge to the drivers does brilliant things to the bass too, which is beyond impressive given the size.

Audio quality is seriously impressive here and you may be surprised by how often you reach for it. I heartily recommend plugging in a hi-res streaming (24-bit/48 kHz) source via USB-C and enjoying all the speaker has to offer.

The app is a basic affair, and some might lament the speaker’s lack of Wi-Fi, but with IP67 protection and 24-hour battery life it’s a great buy when fidelity matters.

Best Party Bluetooth Speaker

Specs

Battery Life Up to 25 hours
Dust/Water Resistance IPX4
Connectivity Bluetooth 6.1, USB-C audio, USB-A, 3.5-mm aux input, two 6.3-mm mic inputs
Special Features AI Karaoke, AI Lighting, app EQ and DJ effects, Auracast, multipoint, replaceable battery
Dimensions 11.73 x 23.38 x 11.56 inches
Weight 25.79 pounds

Part of LG’s xboom collaboration with producer, Black Eyed Peas star, and tech obsessive will.i.am, the Stage 501 is a mighty 25.8-pound party starter. Its 2.2-channel setup combines twin 5.25-inch woofers with two 2.5-inch full-range drivers. Together they’re capable of 160 watts on battery or 220 watts plugged in. In simpler terms: It easily filled a huge workshop space with rave-ready bass, and enough volume for a proper party.

What surprised me more than the party capabilities was that it also sounds acceptable at low volume in my office. I was expecting a pint-sized PA system, but dialled back to casual listening volume and it remained composed. Often, speakers designed for loud really struggle with quiet, and just sound muddy, but that wasn’t the case here. Yes, it prefers it when people are dancing, but it manages well when you’re chilling out too.

The xboom app is excellent, with EQ, AI Karaoke, synchronized lighting, and some cheesy but irresistible DJ punch buttons. LG has also included two very sensible smartphone/tablet stands that position your device at the perfect angle for karaoke nights. It comes with two mic inputs, but you will need to buy microphones separately.

Battery life is “up to” 25 hours, and the battery itself is replaceable. It’s big, and not as grown-up sounding as the Soundbox Mix, but it is cheaper and has a surprisingly good LED light show feature that I expected to hate, but didn’t. Party on dudes.

Honorable Mentions

Bang & Olufsen Beosound A1 (Gen 3) for $399: Gorgeously designed, flawlessly finished, and one of the most covetable Bluetooth speakers around. The brushed aluminum puck has barely changed since 2016, which says plenty about the strength of Cecilie Manz’s original design. The latest version adds a richer, more powerful 360-degree sound from its 3.25-inch woofer, 0.6-inch tweeter, and 60 watts of amplification. It is IP67 rated, lasts up to 24 hours, and is appreciably more repairable and upgradable. I love it, but it’s just a little too expensive when the KEF Muo exists and sounds as good as it does.

Soundboks Mix for $799: The 21.4-pound Soundboks Mix is tremendously loud, with a 10-inch woofer, 1.2-inch tweeter, and 40-hour replaceable battery. WIRED writer Parker Hall measured 111 decibels from a meter away, and was surprised at how musical it remained rather than just battering you with volume. IP65 protection, sturdy handles, and rubberized tennis-ball style corners make it particularly well suited to outdoor parties. It’s expensive and heavy compared to the new breed of party speakers from brands like LG and Sony, but it is superb at what it does.

JBL Charge 6 for $150: It’s just too big to be our absolute favorite Bluetooth speaker, but it was a close run thing between two superb JBL options. The great sound and portability of the Flip 7 won out, but the 40 watts from the Charge 6 deliver more bass and scale, while maintaining detail. Battery life stretches to 24 hours, and you also get IP68 protection, Auracast, app EQ, USB-C lossless playback, and reverse charging. Currently on sale too, making it a real bargain at $150.

Bose SoundLink Plus for $269: Sitting neatly between Bose’s little Flex and chunky Max, the Bose SoundLink Plus weighs 3.37 pounds but produces surprisingly substantial sound, with excellent detail, robust bass, and plenty of power without any rawness at volume. IP67 protection is solid, the 20-hour battery is replaceable, and it can also charge your phone over USB-C. There’s multipoint Bluetooth, app EQ, stereo pairing, and aptX Adaptive for Android too. It takes an irritating five hours to recharge, however. Bose could do with a refresh soon, as the competition has caught up with them.

Sonos Roam 2 for $179: The Sonos Roam 2 is a superb little speaker and if the hugely versatile Sonos Play didn’t exist, it would be one of my top picks. It lacks a bit of punch and scale compared to the larger option, but can still be connected over Wi-Fi or Bluetooth, so it remains ideal at home, in the garden, or out and about. IP67 protection means beach sand and bathroom splashes aren’t a concern. Battery life is a meager 10 hours, though, and it costs considerably more than similarly sized Bluetooth-only rivals, but if you’re a Sonos fan, you won’t be disappointed.

Ultimate Ears Megaboom 4 for $200: If you don’t mind something a bit large, the 9-inch tall Megaboom 4 is one of the best outdoor speakers you can get, according to former WIRED writer Ryan Waniata. It blasts sound in 360-degrees, with enough bass in every direction to please most listeners. It’s also IP67 dust and waterproof, and it floats, making it especially suited to pool and beach days. Like other Ultimate Ears speakers, you can pair multiple Megaboom 4s together through the app and adjust settings like EQ.

Beats Pill for $150: Remember the Beats Pill? WIRED loved the revived 2024 model when it launched, and it remains an excellent choice if you’re wedded to Apple’s ecosystem. You get one-touch pairing, Find My support, and a friction-free setup Apple does so well. Android gets similarly easy pairing and Find My Device support too. Sound is unmistakably Beats, with crisp treble, impressive clarity, and a whole pile of bass, although there’s still no EQ adjustability (you need to use your streaming service’s settings) to tame some occasional brightness. The 24-hour battery, IP67 protection, reverse USB-C charging, lossless playback over USB-C, and stereo pairing keep it competitive, especially since it’s often on sale.

entries.title: ‘Killmonger Locs’ Are Everywhere in Video Games. This Artist Is Sick of It
entries.summary: The Black Panther villain’s hairstyle has become a default for Black video game characters because it’s easy to code. Danielle Udogaranya is changing that.
entries.content:
When the life-simulation game Paralives was released in early access, Danielle Udogaranya’s hand ached at the thought of making new Black hairstyles for it.

It wasn't because she didn't want to create for the game. Udogaranya, better known as Ebonix, has spent over a decade creating custom content for life-simming games with the goal of helping people see themselves on digital screens. Her hesitation stemmed from the physical toll it takes to craft the perfect digital coil, braid, and kink—painstakingly long hours and tedious precision.

“I thought to myself, why am I still having to do this?” Udogaranya, a technical artist who has a degree in psychology, tells WIRED.

Fans of games like The Sims spend time flipping through her sites, downloading custom hair packs inspired by real-life styles not otherwise available in-game. As of now, the Ebonix Patreon has over 115,000 members, and hundreds of both free and paid content items.

The reason behind the demand for custom content in life-simming games is both simple and disappointing: Natural Black hairstyles have been historically underrepresented, and the technology used to make them has been slow to improve.

“With new games coming out now, I'm still seeing the issues, and I'm still seeing the ‘Killmonger locs.’ God forbid we get more than three options,” Udogaranya says, in reference to the stiff, short-dreaded style featured by Michael B. Jordan’s character in Black Panther that became a go-to for many games as well as some other films. Similar examples can be seen in old and new franchises alike, including Tekken 8, Spider-Man 2, Apex Legends, Horizon Zero Dawn, and more. The reason for this Black hair default? Textured hairstyles in games have been reliant on code that was not made for them.

“If you're making straight hair, it’s very easy to taper the ends and then make it cute,” Udogaranya explains. “But when you’re trying to add a black texture on it, it looks like a hot dog.” Thus, immovable, cylindrical “Killmonger locs” are simpler to make than other natural styles.

Black hair in video games has long been a design afterthought—at best—since some of the first Black characters entered the scene. In early 8-bit era games, like SEGA’s Heavyweight Champ, which came out in 1976, Black hairstyles appeared to emphasize minstrel-like stereotypes. During the rise of fighting games in the ’80s and ’90s, where more characters per game were introduced, Black hair was limited because Black player selections were limited. For example, in Street Fighter, there was only one Black character out of the 12 options. When The Sims came out in 2000, the game allowed limited customization, with hair swatches connected to different face options. Though the game allowed for three skin-tone swatches—fair, medium, and dark—natural hairstyle options were virtually nonexistent.

In the decades that followed, 3D animation and customization in gaming continued to flourish, but Black hair has trended toward only a handful of swatches, most of which provided little to minimal movement. However, there have been efforts to tackle this industrywide issue. Dove and Open Source Afro Hair Library launched Code My Crown in 2023, which provides a “complete and free guide for coding textured hair and protective styles in video games,” according to a press release. And, while most of the natural hairstyles in The Sims 4 come from expansion and stuff packs costing around $10 to $40 each, EA has begun to release free downloadable content for players looking to diversify hairstyles. Its latest DLC provides one new natural hairstyle with its pack of six outfits.

Despite these pushes, Udogaranya wanted to make natural hair creation easier and more user-friendly. “After doing some research, and looking at all of the hair tools that are available still to this day, Black hair has just been accommodated in tools that are primarily created for straight hair.”

Udogaranya came across the scholarly paper Curly-Cue: Geometric Methods for Highly Coiled Hair. Published in 2024, it presented new coding techniques to improve both the look and movement of Black hair in 3D animation. With this insight, Udogaranya coded a plug-in for Blender—the free, open-source 3D creation app she normally uses to make custom content.

The Loc & Kinky Strand Generator Tool allows fellow custom content creators to make textured styles that normally could take weeks in under an hour. In just a few clicks, a user can switch from a curl to a coil to a loc. Udogaranya trained her own local AI to assist with automating the processes she did by hand and to fine-tune the code, but no generative AI was used. To use the tool, creators still have to design by hand and can’t type in prompts to generate their styles.

“The whole point of [the Loc & Kinky Strand Generator] tool is that when you do go to draw a strand or apply the actual modifier to a strand, it immediately gives you that kink,” Udogaranya says.

Though the life-sim gaming industry has struggled with diversity, there have been efforts for improvement—in some cases, thanks to Udogaranya herself. In addition to making custom content, she has also served as a gaming consultant for The Sims 4, Life by You, and Love Island: The Game. For other IPs, such as Paralives, Udogaranya notes that there is a shift in interest for Black hair inclusion. Because of this, Udogaranya hopes to eventually make the Blender add-on an independent app and create a licensable version. She tells WIRED that there has been interest from creators for games like Paralives, Roblox, and Second Life, as well as from game developers like Triple-A studios.

The tool is still under development but has been undergoing beta testing. Udogaranya says the test feedback has been “overwhelmingly positive.” Elements of the tool are also patent-pending.

Udogaranya hopes her tool will help eliminate the time, effort, and monetary barriers both content creators and game developers have when it comes to Black hair representation in games. “There’s limitations on the exploration of your identity and self-love and self-worth when the tools that you need are genuinely just missing,” she says. “ I'm ready to get rid of all of that and provide the absolute basic identity identifiers when it comes to games and animation.”

entries.title: 9 Windows Laptops That Give MacBooks a Run for Their Money
entries.summary: Windows laptops have never been so good, and they’re only going to get better as we move through 2026.
entries.content:
Featured in this article

The fight between MacBooks and Windows laptops has never been tighter. There are now more competent alternatives to every MacBook in the lineup. Whether you're choosing Windows because you don't use Apple, you need it for certain software, or just because you like the variety of hardware options, there are tons of great Windows laptops to choose from right now.

I've already tested dozens of Windows laptops this year, and have been reviewing laptops for over a decade. These are my recommendations you can buy right now, including many that were recently refreshed.

For more laptop recommendations, check out our Best 2-in-1 Laptops, Best Gaming Laptops, and Best Budget Laptops. Meanwhile, our overall Best Laptops guide includes the Best Chromebooks and Best MacBooks, too. Still unsure? Read our guide on How to Choose the Right Laptop.

Updated September 2026: I've added the Dell XPS 13, HP OmniBook 5, HP OmniBook Ultra, Lenovo IdeaPad Slim 5x, and Alienware 15. I've also moved some older picks to the honorable mentions section at the bottom.

Other Windows Laptops to Consider

Dell 14 Plus: This laptop sold for hundreds less throughout 2025. And yet, even at around $1,000, I still find it a really solid deal. I do think the XPS 13 is better in a number of ways, especially the display quality and sleek design. However, the extra ports on the Dell 14 Plus are handy, and some may appreciate the slightly larger screen. It also has an upper hand with twice the storage as the Dell XPS 13 and Surface Laptop 7th Edition.

Surface Laptop 7th Edition: I waited a long time for a Windows machine like this Surface Laptop, which came out in 2024—something that could truly compete with the MacBook Air, and it does. The Snapdragon X2 Elite version of the Surface Laptop is available and should provide extra performance. It’s much more expensive at $1,600, which feels overpriced. It occasionally drops to under $1,400, however, which is closer to what the original model sells for. One caveat: You might come across the Surface Laptop 13, which came out in 2025 and is cheaper. I haven't tested that one, but it lacks some of the features I like in the 7th Edition, such as the 3:2 screen.

Lenovo LOQ 15: For many months, the LOQ 15 (8/10, WIRED Recommended) was one of the only gaming laptops under $1,000 that came with an RTX 5060 graphics card. The price has since risen significantly. Yet, it's still a laptop I recommend, as others have also increased in price. And unlike other cheaper gaming laptops, the LOQ 15 has a higher-quality display that's both bright and colorful.

Alienware 15 Gaming Laptop: Speaking of cheaper gaming laptops, the Alienware 15 falls into many of those same traps. It's thick and chunky, yes, but it also has a lower-quality display than you might expect for the price. But it delivers decent performance, has a nice design, and offers the option of an RTX 5050 graphics card. However, the price has gone up by nearly $600.

Surface Pro 12: Unfortunately, if you're looking for a Windows tablet or 2-in-1, your options are slim. There's a newer Surface Pro 13.8 with one of the Snapdragon X2 chips, which are quite expensive. And the detachable keyboard cover (that you should absolutely buy) doesn't come bundled. That's why, at this point, the smaller (and now cheaper) Surface Pro 12 is what most people should buy.

Asus Zenbook S 16: Windows laptops haven't always been known for being lookers. The Asus Zenbook S 16 undoes that stereotype. This thing is absolutely gorgeous, and not in a way that tries to mimic the MacBook. It has its own aesthetic with its white "ceraluminum" material, and I love it. It's also remarkably thin, has an expansive touchpad, and a sharp OLED display—the complete package. The only problem is that the Zenbook S 16 is quite expensive, and prices haven't dropped as much as I hoped. For a smaller model, check out the Zenbook S 14, which is very similar, except it uses an Intel chip instead.

What to Look For in a Windows Laptop

You'll want to read our extensive guide on How to Choose the Right Laptop, but for the basics, decide what category of laptop you need. Most people should buy a 13-inch or 14-inch laptop, and spending around $750 to $1,000 is a good place to start. At this price, you should expect good battery life, a decent screen, solid performance for basic tasks, and a comfortable keyboard and touchpad. You should also expect at least 16 GB of RAM and 512 GB of storage. Anything more than that gets into premium territory where you're paying for higher specs, more performance, or extra features. If you want a discrete GPU for gaming or creative workflows, you'll need to spend more.

A laptop like the Dell 14 Plus is a great example of what you can get in this price range. You can even find laptops with OLED panels and up to one terabyte of storage, depending on how good the discounts are. I would consider anything under $750 a cheap laptop, and it will come with significant compromises, especially in panel and touchpad quality. Fortunately, laptops that use the Qualcomm Snapdragon X chip get great battery life, even when they fall under $750, such as the HP OmniBook 5 14.

Here's a list of important specs to consider:

CPU: Thanks to the huge variety of good chip options, it's never been trickier to buy a laptop. For thin-and-light laptops, I would recommend one of the following chips:

  • Qualcomm Snapdragon X, Snapdragon X Plus, or Snapdragon X Elite
  • Qualcomm Snapdragon X2, Snapdragon X2 Plus, or Snapdragon X2 Elite
  • Intel Core Ultra 225 V or Core Ultra 7 258V
  • Intel Core 5 320, Core Ultra 7 365, or Core Ultra X7 358H

There are many variations of these chips, so you'll undoubtedly run across other strings of numbers, especially on the Intel front. But the above is a good place to start. There’s lots more to say in the world of gaming laptops or content creation devices, so make sure to read our full guide to How to Buy a Gaming Laptop.

GPU: As of now, Intel's Panther Lake X7 or X9 chips have the most powerful integrated graphics. You'll find them in laptops like the Dell XPS 14, which can replicate discrete GPU-level performance like the RTX 4050. Unlike many laptops with discrete GPUs, though, Panther Lake X chips offer great battery life, making them better Windows alternatives to the MacBook Pro.

For discrete options, you'll want one of the latest Nvidia RTX 50-series GPUs, such as the RTX 5060. The biggest leap in performance is between the RTX 5070 and the RTX 5070 Ti, which increases VRAM to 12 GB.

RAM (or memory): Stick with at least 16 GB if you can. Since the Copilot+ designation was introduced in 2024, it has become the new standard. You'll even find laptops as cheap as $600 that have 16 GB of memory. Gamers and content creators should upgrade to 32 GB if possible, though the ongoing memory shortage makes this more expensive. There's been a new surge in 8 GB options, such as the Dell XPS 13, but these should be reserved for only light usage.

Storage: Similar to memory, many laptops have moved to 512 GB as the new standard, and you'll find lots of affordable laptops with that as the base configuration. Upgrading to 1 or 2 terabytes, where possible, will make your life that much easier, especially since many laptops don't offer expandable storage.

Display: Laptops are usually categorized by screen size, with 13-inch, 14-inch, and 16-inch being the most common. Consider size, resolution, refresh rate, and panel type.

Portability: Aside from display size, chassis thickness and weight are the main factors, determining how portable a laptop is to travel with. Other dimensions are important too, but more often than not, that is determined by the screen size.

Ports: Many laptops are limited to USB-C and a headphone jack these days, with some exceptions that include USB-A or HDMI. Make sure your laptop has what you need, or you'll need a USB Hub or laptop docking station to add ports or increase external display support.

Windows 11 vs. Windows 10: What Are the Differences?

If you haven't heard, if you're still on Windows 10, you're no longer getting security updates—at least not without paying extra. If you're wondering what to expect in a new laptop that runs Windows 11, here's a breakdown of the major changes:

Interface: The Start Menu is now centered in the Taskbar and looks a bit different. Visually, it's quite different, but it still functions the same, offering you quick access to applications and documents. Beyond the Start Menu, just about every app will have a different visual flair, with rounded corners and a streamlined aesthetic. While you can still do what you could in Windows 10, things like Settings, Notifications, and System Tray will feel different. You'll also find a new Widgets tray you can activate on the left side of the Taskbar. Unfortunately, you can no longer move the Taskbar to a different side of the screen.

Hardware requirements: This is where most of the frustration around Windows 11 stems from. No one likes being forced to buy new hardware, and while requirements like having at least 4 GB of RAM or 64 GB of storage seem straightforward, the need for a security chip called TPM 2.0 has forced a lot of Windows 10 users to upgrade otherwise good motherboards and CPUs just to move to an operating system they didn't want to begin with.

Performance features: There are tons of new features that help Windows 11 play nicer with accessories and third-party software. One of my favorite examples is HDR support. Windows 11 finally fixes the HDR problem that made using a proper HDR monitor so troublesome, especially in games using Auto HDR. Speaking of games, Windows 11 has features like Game Mode, DirectStorage, and optimizations for windowed games, all of which make for a faster, smoother PC gaming experience.

Is Now a Good Time to Buy?

Laptop prices have been increasing all year, thanks to the memory shortage. In many cases, that means the same laptops cost hundreds of dollars more on any given day. For example, the Dell 14 Plus currently sells for around $1,000, which isn't a terrible price for the configuration. But it was consistently selling for between $650 and $750 for most of 2025. That said, I don't think prices will drop anytime soon. The future of memory pricing is unknown, but many analysts and manufacturers say it will at least last through next year and possibly into 2028.

So yes, there are tons of good options to choose from right now at reasonable prices. All the newest models with the latest chips from Intel, Qualcomm, and AMD are finally out in the wild, along with plenty of good options from 2025. You can always wait for a big sales event like Black Friday, but the savings on specific laptops may not be as big as you might assume. The only significant new hardware we're waiting to see later this year are the new Nvidia RTX Spark laptops. A lot is still unknown about these devices, but they are slated for a fall 2026 release window.
